introFa: کتاب «Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World» نوشته Niall Ferguson یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.

واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Review Article Is Everything Empire? Is Empire Everything? Alexander J Motyl Niall Ferguson, Empire: The Rise and Demise of the British World Order and the Lessons for Global Power, New York, Basic Books, 2002. Niall Ferguson, Colossus: The Price ofAmerica s Empire, New York, Penguin Press, 2004. Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Empire, Cambridge, Mass., Harvard University Press, 2000. Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Multitude, New York, Penguin Press, 2004. Empire is a growth business these days. Amazon lists 10,513 books with empire in the title on its website; Barnes and Noble lists 10,210.1 Whatever the exact number of books that deal with empires as specifically political entities, empire clearly qual ifies as a "hot ticket" item for scholars, journalists, pundits, policymakers, advertis ers, and many others. When a word comes to dominate discourse, it has become a cultural phenomenon. But is empire also real? It is hard to imagine that things were not always this way. Although historians have a long track record of studying past empires, social scientists began devoting substantial attention to empire only in the 1950s and 1960s, when European imperial rule in Africa and Asia crumbled.2 In the 1970s and 1980s interest in empire waned. Ideological critics of the two superpowers excoriated Soviet and American imperial ism.3 Some political scientists explored the rise and fall of great powers.4 Few social scientists studied imperial systems.5 This situation changed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when the collapse of the Soviet Union sparked a lively interest in empire.6 And a sea change took place after 2001, when seemingly everyone, from the far right to the far left, began applying the imperial logo to the United States of President George W Bush. That empire in general and American empire in particular should be so closely asso ciated with the actions of just one American administration in the three years after September 11, 2001, is good reason to be suspicious about the ubiquity of empire-and 229 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 the utility of the concept. Can a full-blown American empire really have emerged in such a short time? Was there really no American empire worth its salt before President Bush's inauguration, or before America's response to September 11 and subsequent invasion of Iraq? The answers to these questions are partly empirical, but mostly con ceptual. An American empire exists if there is an entity that shares the defining charac teristics of other entities called empire.7 An American empire does not exist if there is no entity that shares those defining characteristics. Such commonsensical propositions are embarrassingly obvious, yet, if they are not heeded, the result is confusion. Which is worse, that a senior advisor to President Bush should say, "We're an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality," or that his interlocutor should take such mean ingless blather at face value?8 Policymakers are not the only ones to be confused. Although Niall Ferguson and Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri disagree about almost everything, they have one thing in common: their theories rest on conceptual quicksand. Ferguson writes as a historian; Hardt and Negri write as philosophers. Ferguson's account is full of real people, real places, and real passions; Hardt and Negri's is devoid of them. Ferguson is a materialist who explores the rise and fall of the British and American empires in terms of actual material conditions in the real world; Hardt and Negri are metaphysi cians who produce a relentlessly idealist account of the emergence of "Empire" and the "multitude." Ferguson is open to possibilities and contingencies; Hardt and Negri provide a teleological and functionalist master narrative. Ferguson is a neorealist; Hardt and Negri are postrnodernists. Ferguson is a neoconservative; Hardt and Negri are Communists. Ferguson writes intelligibly for a policymaking audience; Hardt and Negri write unintelligibly for a postmodernist audience. For Ferguson global capitalism is the highest stage of liberal imperialism; for Hardt and Negri Empire is the highest stage of capitalism. Despite these differences, a close reading will show that Ferguson and Hardt and Negri are equally confused about empire and that they converge on proving the very opposite of what they intended to prove. Is Everything Empire? Both of Ferguson's books, as just about everything he has written in recent years, amount to one proposition: the United States should be an empire. In fact, Empire proceeds from the claim that the British Empire was a vehicle for globalization and the dissemination of liberal institutions: "no organization in history has done more to promote the free movement of goods, capital and labour than the British Empire in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. And no organization has done more to impose Western norms of law, order and governance around the world."9 According to Ferguson, most British colonies benefited from free trade and liberal democratic institutions. The British made many awful mistakes, but by and large the ledger is 230 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Alexander J Motyl positive. The United States is also an empire. Like that of the British, the American empire is committed to globalization, free trade, and liberal institutions. It would be good for the world, and especially its failed or failing states, for the United States to exert imperial rule and promote free trade and liberal institutions. Unfortunately, the United States seems incapable of doing so. It suffers from a fiscal crisis, an unwill ingness on the part of its best and brightest to administer colonies, and a dreadfully short attention span. An "empire in denial," the United States should wake up and be the empire that it can and should be. Colossus picks up this thread and attempts to show how a small republic on the eastern seaboard became an expansionist country that engulfed most of the conti nent, a hegemon and reluctant imperialist abroad, a superpower during the cold war, and a hyperpower and empire after the USSR's collapse. Regardless of whether or not the United States currently is or should be an empire, Ferguson does a fine job demonstrating that imperialism, expansion, and empire building have been part and parcel of American discourse and behavior since the country's founding. But the goal of Colossus is to demonstrate systematically what Empire argued only in pass ing-that liberal empire, possibly in general and certainly in the case of its British variant, can be a transmitter of capitalism and democracy. Ferguson takes great pains not to say that all empires were equally benign. He contrasts the British Empire with those of the Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, French, Belgians, and especially Japanese and finds that the liberal British Empire was on balance good for the colonized peo ples and, in any case, that it was certainly better than alternative forms of imperial rule.10 And he does have a point. If one is to be ruled by an empire, better that it be liberal and democratic than illiberal and authoritarian. Besides, the process of intro ducing capitalism and democracy has involved great hardship, exploitation, and bloodshed everywhere, even in the imperial metropoles. "The question is not whether British imperialism was without a blemish. It was not. The question is whether there could have been a less bloody path to modernity. Perhaps in theory there could have been. But in practice?""II All in all, then, liberal empire worked. Whereas Empire is uniformly upbeat about the effects of liberal empire, Colossus takes a more nuanced approach. Ferguson sticks to his thesis that liberal empire is a good thing, but he grapples with the question why British rule in India did so little to benefit it economically-in marked contrast to Singapore, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. His counterfactual answer, that the British were insufficiently imperial in imposing free trade and the market on India, is logically consistent with his larger argu ment and has the merit of being open to empirical testing.'2 Naturally, if one is intrinsi cally opposed to empire and globalization, no amount of counterfactual logic or evi dence suggesting that they facilitate markets and democracy is likely to be persuasive. Ferguson's emphasis on the legacies of empire is especially useful. As the USSR's collapse has demonstrated, the postcommunist states have all been burdened, to vari ous degrees, by Communist imperial institutions. As a general rule, those that expe 231 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 rienced Communism and empire longest and most deeply-such as the vast majority of the Soviet republics-have experienced the greatest difficulty in adopting democ ratic and market-oriented institutions. Those that felt the grip of Communism and empire least-such as the East-Central European states that were admitted into the European Union in May 2004-have had the fewest such difficulties.13 Imperial legacies matter, and Ferguson is right to suggest that the legacies can be positive as well as negative. They may not be positive across the board and to the same degree: the differences between India and Canada stand out and require an explanation. But the overall differences among the British successor states are, as Ferguson correctly suggests, less than those between them and the successor states of other, less liberal, empires. The Fall of Empire Although Empire tells a good story, it signally fails to make the case for an American empire. It fails partly because Ferguson devotes only the conclusion to his plea and mostly because he is not quite sure what he means by empire. As Ferguson does not even define the concept, at most one can surmise from his discussion of British and American power that empire entails "actually ruling a colony" by means of "colonial structures."'14 Ruling stands in sharp contrast to the "American approach [which] has too often been to fire some shells, march in, hold elections and then get the hell out-until the next crisis."15 Ferguson also believes that, while America's "informal empire" is an "empire of multinational corporations, of Hollywood movies and even of Television evangelists," the United States "lacks the drive to export its capital, its people and its culture to those backward regions which need them most urgently and which, if they are neglected, will breed the greatest threats to its security."16 But if multinational corporations, Hollywood, and television evangelists export capital, people, and culture wherever there are markets for their products, then talk of some absent "drive" is either misplaced or wrong. To muddy the waters even more, Ferguson concludes the book with a ringing call to the United States to admit that it already is an empire. "It is an empire, in short, that dare not speak its name. It is an empire in denial."17 Even if one agrees with Ferguson that the British Empire promoted free trade and democratic institutions and that the United States is, or should admit to being, an empire, does it therefore follow that the American empire can or should proceed in the British Empire's footsteps? Not at all. First, it is an unwarranted leap in logic to conclude from the British example that all liberal empires can promote free trade and democratic institutions. The initial conditions underpinning British success may no longer be present. Second, Ferguson persuasively demonstrates that Britain's informal (or indirect) rule became formal (or direct) unwittingly and unintentionally.18 If Britain's experi ence is a guide to America's, then it follows that the United States should not pur 232 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

AlexanderJ Motyl posefully convert indirect rule into direct rule but wait for that to happen, naturally and in the course of time. Third, even if it is granted Ferguson that the United States should aim for direct rule, could America actually succeed in establishing a formal empire? It is surely true that the constraints on direct rule are much greater today than they were in the heyday of Britannia. Indeed, they may be so much greater as to be insuperable. The British Empire's successful dissemination of democratic and liberal norms means that the United States could never employ force, coercion, and violence to the same degree that Britain was able to employ them in the past. These norms would con strain Americans' own behavior, and they would also limit the degree to which potential colonies, their neighbors, other states, and the international community would be willing to tolerate American interventions. The example of Iraq-even if it is granted that the United States was motivated by the declarative reasons employed by the Bush administration-suggests as much. In other words, the American empire might be able to get away with a few instances of using force to spread markets and democracy, but it is hard to imagine that it could do more than that. If so, the empire would either quickly reach its limits and include at most one or two colonies-surely a far less grandiose outcome than Ferguson has in mind-or it would be forced to retreat, thereby letting globalization and democratic dissemination take care of them selves. Fourth, it is hardly self-evident that, today, empire is the most efficient means of disseminating the benefits of free trade and liberal institutions. Just because the British Empire may have been a vehicle of globalization and liberalism, it does not follow that, today, only empire can promote globalization and liberalism. Nor does it follow that, today, only liberal empire can promote globalization and empire. Indeed, globalization may have its own dynamic-not the least of which is the power of the Internet and financial flows-and democracies have surely multiplied without American or any other kind of imperial intervention.19 In sum, there is no reason to think that an American empire is the only or even the best means to promote global ization and liberalism. Last, even if empire is the most efficient means of disseminating free trade and democracy, there is no reason to think that such a project is possible in the failed and failing states Ferguson believes would most benefit from American intervention. Such states need order and stability first. Even if empires are best suited to fix bro ken states-a dubious claim that Ferguson wisely refrains from making-America's alarmingly incompetent performance in postwar Iraq suggests that, even now, the United States continues to be ill-suited to abandon the "American approach" Ferguson derides. And even if that performance miraculously improves, the vast expenditure of military and financial resources that pacifying Iraq involves should lead one to doubt that the United States could fix another broken state anytime soon. 233 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 The Collapse of Colossus Colossus takes the conceptual bull by the horns and attempts to address the definitional issues that led to the fall of Empire. Ferguson knows that simply calling the United States an empire will not do. After all, all his theoretical and policy claims hinge on the United States' being an empire. In particu lar, Ferguson understands that he must be able to distinguish empire from hege mon.20 Ferguson imagines that, if hegemony and empire are assumed to be different, it could follow that "a hegemon can be more powerful than empire."'21 Such a con clusion strikes him as "paradoxical," by which he means that the original distinction, between hegemony and empire, must therefore be invalid. The "distinction between hegemony and empire would be legitimate if the term empire did simply mean...direct rule over foreign territories without any political representation of their inhabitants."22 But "imperial history" is more complex. Just how complex is evident from the "simple typology" he proposes: seven columns consisting of four to eight different kinds of imperial characteristics (metro politan system, self-interested objectives, public goods, method of rule, economic system, cui bono?, and social character).23 In effect, Ferguson asks the reader to pick a dish from each column and thereby produce a different kind of empire. A simple mathematical calculation shows that his menu results in 184,320 possible combina tions!24 If these combinations are all different empires, then the United States is obviously an empire, but so too are France, Germany, Russia, Israel, India, China, Japan, Indonesia, Albania, Estonia, and every other country. Indeed, every imagin able political system under the sun is an empire, from Thebes to Topeka. Ferguson is right to say that imperial history is complex, but this complexity is precisely why catch-all categories are useless and clear conceptual distinctions are necessary. Direct rule means that representatives of the imperial center govern colo nial peripheries. Indirect rule means that native administrators under the control of the center govern the colonial peripheries. Under both forms of rule peripheries do not engage in or pursue foreign relations. Hegemony entails neither direct nor indi rect rule. Instead, hegemonic rule means only that some one state exerts substantial influence on the foreign affairs of another.25 Because Ferguson the neorealist is obsessed with power, he fails to see that direct rule, indirect rule, and hegemony are not just about power.26 All big and powerful states exert power and force other enti ties to bend to their will. When metropoles rule directly and indirectly, however, their colonies are administrative territories and not formally sovereign states. In contrast, when great powers exert hegemony, the objects of that hegemony are formally sover eign states that adjust their behavior accordingly.27 Thus, while both empire (direct and indirect rule) and hegemony involve power, the imperial relationship implicating a center and a periphery is qualitatively different from a hegemonic relationship implicating two states. Ferguson can not countenance the eminently sensible distinction between empire 234 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

AlexanderJ Motyl and hegemony for a more practical reason. If he accepted this distinction, his argu ment that the United States is an empire but refuses to act like one would be absurd. Ferguson's argument rests on the so-called paradox of America's both being and refusing to behave like an empire. If there is no paradox, there is no argument and no policy prescription. And if the United States really is a hegemon, then it logically follows that it can not be faulted for not acting like an empire. This painfully com monsensical conclusion destroys the raison de'tre of Ferguson's books. Ferguson's conceptual confusion reaches its apotheosis in the second half of Colossus.28 There it is argued that the United States may now be an empire in decline. Why? Ferguson cites three reasons. Its looming economic difficulties may not permit the United States to sustain its imperial reach; its citizens are unwilling to settle in and administer or rule colonies; and the country has an insufficiently long attention span, preferring to intervene and then leave as soon as possible.29 It is clear from these three reasons that, notwithstanding his protestations, Ferguson really does view empire as direct rule. A financial crisis might weaken American hegemony, but it would be unlikely to shake it to its foundations. And a manpower shortage and a short attention span have nothing to do with hegemony and everything to do with direct rule. Ferguson wants to have it both ways. He believes that the United States already is an empire, to be able to claim that it is in decline, but at the same time he argues that its evident incapacity to be an effective empire is responsible for its inability to be an empire. But if the United States is not an empire, then it can not be in decline. And if the United State is a "hegemonic empire," then it can not be faulted for lacking the defining characteristics of a directly ruled empire. Which is it? Is the United States an empire or not? Ferguson acknowledges that the United States has, at least since its pursuit of nineteenth-century expansionism on the North American continent, been extremely reluctant to rule and acquire territories abroad and that it does not at present rule directly over any colonies. In a word, Ferguson mistakenly believes that the nonpossession by the United States of the defining characteristics of direct impe rial rule is a cause of decline, whereas nonpossession means only that the United States has no directly ruled empire. Ironically, Ferguson also demonstrates, albeit unwittingly, that the United States should intervene, and thereby act imperially, as little as possible. He persuasively argues that the United States has generally left a mess in the countries in which it has gotten involved for brief periods of time. He also shows that it has been and is reluc tant to expend resources, manpower, and attention on bona fide institution building, except in such cases as post-World War II Germany and Japan, when it had no choice. If so, it follows that the British Empire can not be a model for the United States. Indeed, it might be best for the world if the United States abstained from all but the occasional unavoidable interventions. America's possible abdication of empire worries Ferguson. Were it to abdicate, 235 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 and were other responsible powers such as the European Union to follow suit, the result would be disaster, a Hobbesian war of all against all compounded by state fail ure and other miseries.30 But Ferguson's worries are either unwarranted or pointless. Even if the United States is the only power capable of maintaining law and order in the world, it does not follow that the United State must therefore be an empire. Being a hegemon would surely suffice. And, even if hegemony led to global disaster, it seems pointless to encourage the United States to shoulder direct rule-involving endless interventions and vast expenditure of resources-without much help from its friends and without the desire, energy, ability, or inclination to do so. Is Empire Everything? Like Ferguson, Hardt and Negri make a simple argument. A new global order appears to be emerging: Empire (they insist on the upper case spelling). Like capital ism and power, Empire is the product of historical developments driven by popular desire for freedom and struggles against power. Empire consists of the imperialist United States, other nation-states, the capitalist corporations, and a variety of global institutions. As Empire emerges, so too does its slayer, the multitude. The multitude is not yet a reality, but its contours are already visible. Like Empire, which knows no boundaries, the multitude is potentially open to all humanity; unlike the people, the masses, and the working class, the multitude consists of singularities that share the common. Empire is digging its own grave by empowering the multitude with the very tools-globalization, the eradication of boundaries, mobility-that the multi tude will use to resist Empire and bring it down. The multitude will then create a global democracy, or rule of all by all. Hardt and Negri have produced a standard Marxist text, but with a twist. All Marxists see capitalism as the enemy and the state as its (nonautonomous, more or less autonomous, more or less relatively autonomous, or more or less potentially autonomous) handmaiden. The proletariat will bring down capitalism, and the state will wither away, partly because of its own efforts and the wise guidance of Communists, but mostly because of the dynamics of capitalism itself, which must, sooner or later, collapse. There are many variations on this basic theme, but all dis play this grand narrative. In Hardt and Negri's version, capitalism is global capital ism or globalization; the state is Empire; the proletariat is the multitude. Capitalism is exploitative and unsustainable; the state/Empire rests on contradictions; the prole tariat/multitude will come into existence and be empowered; and capitalism/state/Empire will come crashing down if and when the proletariat/multi tude rises up. And the denouement will also be the same: democracy. Hardt and Negri have also written a philosophy of history, but a strikingly unper 236 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Alexander J Motyl suasive one. Philosophies of history invariably ascribe teleology to history, arguing that it must culminate in some present condition or thing.31 In contrast, Hardt and Negri construct their philosophy in terms of something, Empire, that does not yet exist. Their ex post facto interpretation of the past can only make sense in terms of Empire, while Empire can only make sense in terms of this account of historical development. The result is a truly vicious circle. Both books are thus strangely func tionalist: the logic of their teleology demands that things happen as they happened because the future, Empire, required such outcomes. They read history backwards from an imaginary future to an imagined past-and place effects before causes.32 While the point of philosophy may or may not be to interpret or change the world, it should certainly not be to confuse it. The good news is that few outside their circle of interlocutors will look at, let alone comprehend, these books. The damage that Hardt and Negri can inflict on the project of human liberation is thus necessarily limited. But the bad news is that obfuscation is no substitute for a vigorous left, one able to champion causes that the current Zeitgeist ignores or downplays. Like all true believers, Hardt and Negri believe precisely because their faith defines the terms of its own validity. They address their critics in the same spirit. Those who claim that they are anarchists can not appreciate that "the development of the multitude is not anarchic or spontaneous but rather its organization emerges through the collaboration of singular social subjects."33 Those who say they are Leninists can not appreciate that "singularity is not diminished in the common."34 Those who say they are against the workers do not understand that the "hegemony of immaterial labor... should not imply any political hegemony." Those who accuse them of being "failed or incomplete dialectitians" do not appreciate that "the dynam ic of singularity and multiplicity that defines the multitude denies the dialectical alternative between the One and the Many-it is both and neither."35 These refuta tions rest not on data, theory, or logic, but on semantic assertions and theoretical cir cularity. Harvey Cox has noted that proponents of "the market" treat it as if it were a deity.36 For Hardt and Negri, Empire is God, and history is the unfolding of God's will. The Ubiquity of Empire Lest one think that Empire is just an empire, Hardt and Negri assure readers that it decidedly is not. Quite the contrary, they insist that to equate Empire with past empires would be to employ a metaphorical approach. Their approach is conceptual. "We should emphasize that we use 'Empire' here not as a metaphor, which would require demonstration of the resemblances between today's world order and the Empires of Rome, China, the Americas, and so forth, but rather as a concept."37 But Hardt and Negri have it exactly backward. The validity of com paring one empire to other empires is precisely what the concept of empire implies: "empire" presumably refers to a set of entities with defining characteristics that make them empires. What then, if not empire, is Empire? It "is a decentered and 237 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 deterritorializing apparatus of rule that progressively incorporates the entire global realm within its open, expanding frontiers."38 "Empire can only be conceived as a universal republic, a network of powers and counterpowers structured in a boundless and inclusive architecture."39 In sum, Empire is everywhere. It has no center and no periphery. Run of the mill empires, in contrast, are somewhere, and they have cen ters and peripheries. Empire can not be just empire. Empire must be everywhere, because struggles are everywhere and disparate worldwide struggles can be antiimperial only if all their dif ferent targets are subsumed under one catch-all category, Empire. The uprising in Tiananmen Square, the riots in Los Angeles, the strike movements in Paris and Seoul, and the Chiapas rebellion "cannot communicate, because their languages cannot be translated."40 But different and unrelated phenomena can be made similar and related by being counterpoised to an ubiquitous entity that lacks a center. If Empire is equally itself at every point of contact with struggles, then disparate struggles against different things are automatically transformed into a common antiimperial project. Like Empire, the multitude must also be everywhere. Were the multitude not everywhere, disparate struggles in different parts of the world could still be antiimperial, but they would not be the handiwork of a consciously antiimperial entity destined to overcome Empire and build democracy. And because the multitude is everywhere, it must encompass all "sin gularities" and transcend all boundaries. The multitude can not be reduced to some peo ple, class, or group, because these categories are necessarily confined to some defined place and thus could not wage a global struggle. Hardt and Negri's claim that resistance is everywhere, that empire is everything, and that the multitude is everybody amounts to the threefold proposition that every thing explains everything, that everything explains Empire, and that Empire explains everything. These are three variously graded examples of "theories of everything" that, in their grandiosity, effectively explain nothing. The claim that everything explains everything is either trivial-it is sensed by looking at the world and mar veling at its complexity-or impossibly radical: does every thing cause every other thing equally? That everything causes Empire is either a restatement of Hardt and Negri's teleological philosophy of history-that Empire is the end point of all things-or the trivial claim that the totality of reality somehow causes every single thing within that reality. And that Empire causes everything amounts either to a restatement of the functionalism discussed above, in which a nonexistent future Empire requires that history unfold in a manner that necessarily culminates in Empire, or to the theoretically untenable proposition characteristic of all revolution ary ideologies that some one factor-class, race, discourse, power, Empire-holds the key to all reality.41 Although Hardt and Negri insist that Empire has no center or periphery, their attempts to convey how Empire actually works suggest the exact opposite. At one point in Empire they say that the global order can be envisioned as a pyramid. The 238 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Alexander J Motyl apex is the United States, the top tier consists of transnational corporations, the mid dle tier of sovereign nation-states, and the bottom tier of "groups that represent pop ular interests in the global arrangement"-nongovernmental organizations, the media, and the like.42 The image of a pyramid suggests that the global order is hier archical and that its center is tantamount to the apex, the United States. Later in the book, Hardt and Negri even concede that the United States really does appear to be the Empire and that its forms of rule can be associated with New York, Washington, D.C., and Los Angeles.43 Multitude compounds this confusion, while also belying the claim that Empire is everywhere. The structure of the "global body politic," the "nerve center" of which is now in Davos, is no longer that of a pyramid, with the United States at its apex.44 Instead, there are three "levels." The first consists of the global capitalist firms, the second of the nation-states that establish the arena within which they can function, and the third of international institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.45 The first two levels correspond to the first two tiers of the pyra mid, but the third level is out of sync with the third tier. Where does the United States belong? And how do China, India, Brazil, Nigeria, South Africa, and Indonesia, to name just a few large non-European states that are hardly puppets of America, fit in?46 Hardt and Negri have no clue. Indeed, they implicitly acknowl edge as much when they write that power seems to be exercised "as if" it were directed from some imperial center.47 The Limitations of Multitude The multitude, Hardt and Negri tell us, "might thus be conceived as.. .an open and expansive network in which all differences can be expressed freely and equally, a network that provides the means of encounter so that we can work and live in common."48 More to the point, perhaps, "the multitude is a multiplicity of all these singular differences" that partake of "the common that allows them to communicate and act together."49 How are the singular and the com mon related? "We share bodies with two eyes, ten fingers, ten toes; we share life on this earth; we share capitalist regimes of production and exploitation; we share com mon dreams of a better future. Our communication, collaboration, and cooperation, furthermore, not only are based on the common that exists but also in turn produce the common."50 The result is "a spiral, symbiotic relationship....In this spiral each successive movement from the production of subjectivity to the production of the common is an innovation that results in a richer reality."51 Notwithstanding the spi ral, "the multitude needs a political project to bring it into existence."52 That project is revolt, and "revolts mobilize the common in two respects, increasing the intensity of each struggle and extending to other struggles."53 At some point, "the global cycle of struggles develops in the form of a distributed network. Each local struggle func tions as a node that communicates with all the other nodes without any hub or center of intelligence."54 239 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 That this reasoning is deeply flawed should be obvious. Hardt and Negri's first mistake is the happy assumption that the formation of subjectivities will, together with communication and collaboration, necessarily spiral upwards, producing more and more of each. But even if it were true that these "variables" are mutually rein forcing, there is no reason to think that an endless spiral would result. It is just as possible to imagine that a plateau will be reached or that the interaction between subjectivity formation and communication and collaboration will go into reverse. After all, why should it not be possible for the production of signals to result in noise, thereby reducing collaboration and skewing the formation of subjectivities? Second, even if Hardt and Negri are right to suggest that disparate people thanks, no doubt, to their commonality of eyes and ears and noses!-might be able to communicate and collaborate, there is no logical basis for concluding that a global multitude encompassing all humanity is possible. Communication and collaboration and the possession of common physiological features have never been sufficient to overcome human tensions, arguments, conflicts, disagreements, and violence in the past. If the workers of the world, who presumably shared one class interest, failed to unite in any country of the world, why should the multitude be more successful? Third, Hardt and Negri blithely assume that the not-yet-existent multitude will be the benign, interactive collectivity of human beings they want it to be. Two other possibilities can be considered. Since Hardt and Negri insist that power, force, and violence are everywhere, is it not possible that they will continue to be everywhere even after the multitude breaks with Empire? Moreover, since the multitude will have just emerged from centuries of Empire and capitalism, is it not also possible that it will retain certain "habits" and "performative" inclinations that incline some of its more retrograde singularities to continue practicing these, to use a Soviet term, "relics of the past"?55 It is hardly surprising that so fuzzy an actor as the multitude should bring down Empire in an equally fuzzy manner. "When does the moment of rupture come?"56 Hardt and Negri respond to one metaphor with another. "The bowstring shoots the arrow of a new temporality, inaugurating a new future."'57 And just when might this arrow be shot? Hardt and Negri are silent. "A philosophical book like this.. .is not the place for us to evaluate whether the time of revolutionary political decision is imminent....A book like this is not the place either to answer the question 'What is to be done?' That has to be decided concretely in collective political discussions."'58 Is that it? Does the possibility of the multitude's victory rest on the persuasive ness of a mixed metaphor and Hardt and Negri's unwillingness to be pinned down? Not quite. For all their talk of the multitude and its powers of constitution, Hardt and Negri are fully committed to the leading role in any such process for the "militants" who will mobilize and inspire the multitude.59 Here are the makings of the typical Communist dilemma: how to combine the formal recognition of the primacy of the 240 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

AlexanderJ Motyl masses with the practical recognition that, unless mobilized by a smart-thinking van guard, the multitude will not opt for revolution. Indeed, "one fact that should be obvious in all this is that the multitude does not arise as a political figure sponta neously and that the flesh of the multitude consists of a series of conditions that are ambivalent: they could lead toward liberation or be caught in a new regime of exploitation and control."60 Hardt and Negri's postmodernist militants will be speaking a language-post modernism-that is incomprehensible to the multitude. Hardt and Negri also appear to have no sense of how real people lead their lives. Finally, Hardt and Negri ascribe well-nigh magical powers to the multitude. Indeed, Hardt and Negri actually believe that the "subordinate classes organized in revolt" "never entertained any illusions about the legitimacy of state violence....They never forgot that the laws that legiti mate state violence are transcendental norms that maintain the privileges of the dom inant class....They knew that whereas the violence of capital and the state rests on transcendent authority, the legitimation of their class struggle was based solely on their own interests and desires."'6' These three components-a caste-like militant class, ignorance of real people's lives, and the idealization of real people's capabili ties-are a recipe for disaster. Sooner or later Hardt and Negri's militants will be dis appointed by ordinary people, who will never measure up to their hopes for the mul titude. At that point, violence may be unavoidable. Seen in this light, Hardt and Negri's talk of "love" is a bad joke at best and bad faith at worst. How is the multitude to be constituted? "Constituent power.. .is a deployment of force that defends the historical progression of emancipation and lib eration; it is, in short, an act of love."62 "Love means precisely that our expansive encounters and continuous collaborations bring us joy."63 "Love serves as the basis for our political projects in common and the construction of a new society. Without this love, we are nothing."64 When self-styled Communists talk of loving the people, it may be time for the multitude to head for the hills. It may also be time to wonder about their moral obtuseness. Hardt and Negri can not avoid grappling with the fact that every form of actually practiced socialism or communism has produced untold misery and countless deaths.65 Communists such as Hardt and Negri can not just be anti-Stalinist; it is too late for that. If they are not to be apologists for criminal regimes, they have no choice but to be "anticommunist Communists." Can "Hot" Books Be Vacuous? The enormous popularity of empire, like its careless usage, says something impor tant about academic theorizing. Academics are evidently hostage to politics and norms in ways that they are loath to admit. They are prone to exactly the same kind of muddleheaded thinking of which they accuse publics and policymakers. 241 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 Considering how academics flock to fashionable concepts and misuse them for ideo logical reasons, one can not but be pessimistic about the ability of the social sciences to make progress. These four books can, alas, only deepen one's pessimism. All four of these books are deeply flawed. But does not their immense populari ty-Ferguson's among policy experts and Hardt and Negri's among intellectuals and students-belie such a sweeping claim? Not at all. The popularity of social science and humanities texts is a function of various factors, including the stature of the authors, their institutional affiliation, their connections to people in important and influential places, the stature of the press, the extent and effectiveness of its advertis ing campaign, and other such nonintellectual factors. Even the hard sciences, which have far more rigorous standards for judging quality, are subject to external pres sures. And, as should be evident to students of comparative politics, the social sci ences and humanities do not have such commonly agreed-upon standards. Positivists, postpositivists, Marxists, postmodernists, constructivists, and many, many others disagree on what constitutes a legitimate area of inquiry and on the standards by which its quality should be measured. Within such a largely unregulat ed marketplace of ideas, it is small wonder that all kinds of inferior products should be sold as legitimate wares. Sokal's Hoax-in which the physicist Alan Sokal was able successfully to submit a nonsensical, though seemingly postmodernist, interpre tation of physics to the journal Social Text-deprives social scientists of the luxury of assuming that social acceptance necessarily means quality.66 Indeed, there may be good reason to believe the exact opposite-that books become "hot" precisely because they are simplistic in methodology and grandiose in their claims and, as such, meet a need in a public eager for easy answers to difficult questions. One could cite, for example, Samuel P. Huntington's The Clash of Civilizations and Robert Kagan's Of Paradise and Power.67 Huntington presents a caricature of identity politics-as students of ethnicity and nationalism know-and yet the book became wildly popular because its simplistic presentation of complex developments appealed to a policymaking audience in search of bold new paradigms after the end of the cold war. Kagan overlooks all the differences within Europe and America in order to argue that Europeans are from Venus and Americans from Mars, a claim that anyone with even superficial experience with either region knows to be vastly overblown.68 But the book found a large audience precisely because that sim ple message seemed to offer a grand explanation of the deepening transatlantic chasm. Huntington and Kagan, like Ferguson and Hardt and Nergi, provide catchy slogans-Civilizations are clashing! Americans are from Mars! Europeans are from Venus! The American empire is declining! The multitude will defeat Empire!-to confused audiences looking for quick solutions to their existential troubles. Ferguson, Huntington, and Kagan pitch their advertising at policy elites who lost their bearings after the Soviet Union collapsed, the cold war ended, and America became a hyperpower uncertain of how to act in the world. AlexanderJ Motyl ence are crisis-ridden leftists equally shaken by the collapse of the Soviet Union but lacking even a focus, such as the United States, for their aspirations.69 The many other recent books on the so-called American empire provide indirect evi dence of the plausibility of this hypothesis about which books become hot. How many of these books are about a system of rule that shares the defining characteristics of other systems called empires? Chalmers Johnson is really interested in America's military presence and interventions abroad.70 William Odom and Robert Dujarric, John B. Judis, Andrew J. Bacevich, and Emmanuel Todd explore America's hyperpower status and interventionist foreign policy.71 James J. Hentz and his collaborators examine American foreign policy challenges in the twenty-first century.72 Rashid Khalidi excoriates American policy in the Middle East.73 Arundhati Roy engages in a critique of America's involvement in Iraq and globalization.74 What is new here is not the emergence of a bona fide American empire, but the terminological convergence of left and right on a resonant term. Both sides employ empire in reference to the United States, and both more or less agree on the range of chest-beating and tub-thumping American behaviors they have in mind. Thus, the new books on American empire are really either about the causes and consequences of America's hyperpower status or about the assertive foreign policies of the Bush administration. Empire serves only as a convenient tag, a catchy label that, by remaining undefined at a time when powerful neoconservative forces inside or close to the administration make their case for foreign policy activism in exactly the same terms, is all the more capable of attracting readers. But empire's ana lytical utility is close to nil. Empire and Comparative Politics This criticism of Ferguson and Hardt and Negri should not be interpreted as imply ing that students of comparative politics should stay away from empire. Quite the contrary, the confusion surrounding the concept is a call for clearer thinking and bet ter research. The first task before scholars is to define empire in a way that reduces it to a manageable something and not expands it to an unmanageable everything. The second is to employ the concept as a tool for comparing the dynamics of imperial political systems. Fortunately, many serious scholars have already blazed these two trails. As to the first task, scholars of empire generally propose some version of Michael Doyle's definition: "empire...is a relationship, formal or informal, in which one state controls the effective political sovereignty of another political society."75 Although they may disagree on details, scholars agree that empires are political systems con sisting of unequal relations between centers and peripheries and are not just big bad multiethnic states. Thus, empires are potential objects of exploration for students of 243 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 comparative politics. How empires work, how social, economic, political, and cultur al attitudes and behaviors sustain them, and how they decline and collapse are all questions to which comparative politics may have answers. The question of how empires emerge, on the other hand, is one that students of comparative politics will have to share with their colleagues in international relations. As Ferguson rightly notes, empires can emerge without imperialism-or the expansion of states and their forcible annexation of foreign territories. Indeed, empires can emerge in any number of nonimperialist ways involving purchase, dynastic marriage, and internal change.76 As to the second task, excellent works on empire, as a political system, already exist. Karen Barkey and Mark von Hagen's After Empire, Karen Dawisha and Bruce Parrott's End of Empire?, Michael Doyle's Empire, and S. N. Eisenstadt's The Political Systems of Empires, in addition to many other books and articles, all grap ple with empires in a manner that is compatible with and suggestive for comparative politics as a discipline. All these works are careful to define empire, and all examine various aspects of imperial rule in a controlled comparative fashion-from the Roman Empire to the Habsburg Empire to the Soviet Union. Dominic Lieven's recent Empire deserves special mention, both for its quality and its importance to students of comparative politics.77 Lieven provides a historically rich account of the rise and fall of the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, while embedding it in a comparative framework that focuses on the British, Ottoman, and Habsburg realms. Lieven also examines the Roman and Han empires, sensibly con cludes that the United States neither is nor has an empire, and helpfully traces the etymological evolution of the term, "empire." Lieven's historical training and British roots, as well as the book's appearance before September 11 and the Iraq war, may have helped Empire avoid the pitfalls of audience-driven sensationalism. The book is not without its flaws, the most serious of which-at least in terms of the conceptual concerns raised in this article-is Lieven's ambivalence toward con ceptual clarity and its role in explanation. Thus, Lieven claims that "I use the idea of empire as a central organizing principle and a means of comparison between a num ber of great imperial polities." His discussion of whether the United States is or has an empire rests on a fairly clear sense ofjust what all empires have in common: "it is interesting to ask to what extent American power is imperial, in other words similar to the manner in which power was created and applied by the great empires of the past."78 At the same time, Lieven states that "it is absolutely not my intention to set up empire as some sharply precise, all-encompassing concept through which to com prehend present-day polities."79 But that is exactly what Empire does. After all, only a "sharply precise, all-encompassing concept" can identify the "great imperial poli ties" worthy of comparison-and inclusion in a book. Less conceptual ambivalence might have made Lieven's discussion of the United States more rigorous. Alexander J Motyl venient starting point. Is the United States an empire? While it may have engaged, as Ferguson argues, in imperialism in the early nineteenth century and may have been an empire at the time the eastern metropole ruled the western frontier areas, Washington surely does not, today as in the recent past, exert imperial control over the fifty states. Does the United States have an empire? Does it rule colonies, directly or indirectly? In Afghanistan, competing warlords, the United Nations and NATO, which may or may not be pawns of American imperialism, and the government of Hamid Karzai appear to preside over different bits of the country. In Iraq authority is even more fragmented, and, while the United States may be an imperialist or occupier, it can hardly be said to rule. That leaves Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, but, if they comprise the whole American empire, it hardly merits concern. What then of indirect rule? Does the United States control the internal and exter nal affairs or territories through their native administrators? America surely exerted just this kind of rule over many Latin American countries in the past. Today, American soldiers are stationed in many countries, but it would be news to Japan, South Korea, Germany, Kyrgyzstan, and others that Washington actually runs their domestic and foreign policies. American intelligence agencies may still conspire to affect elections and elites, but that is tantamount to saying that American influence is not imperial. Empires can tell their colonies what to do; they need not engage in elaborate subterfuge. Perhaps the American empire is a new type of empire, one completely unique and unlike any other empire of the past.80 But if the American empire really is a new type of empire, then it must possess the defining characteristics of all other empires. As such, it would, as an empire, be identical to all other empires, as empire is the genus to which all types of empire belong. The only difference between the uniquely American imperial type and all other empires could only be that, as a new type, it would have to differ from them in terms of nonessential, nondefining characteristics. Alternatively, if the United States really is completely unlike all past empires, then the American empire can not be an empire.81 If empire is ruled out, only hegemony is left. Is the United States a global hege mon? Is it a hyperpower or a superpower or just a very, very big power? Does the United States exert substantial influence on the foreign affairs of other states? The answer to all these questions is some form of yes.82 Hegemony may or may not be good, and such overbearing behavior may be aggressive, unjust, wrong, stupid, immoral, exploitative, evil, and imperialist, but it is not imperial. Secretary of State Donald H. Rumsfeld's remark, "We don't do empire," was unwitting testimony to that distinction.83 By using the verb "do," Rumsfeld was denying, not that the United States is or has an empire, but that its policies-what it did-were aggressive, unjust, and so on.84 245 All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

Comparative Politics January 2006 Conclusion There is no need for students of comparative politics to reinvent the wheel. The study of empire not only exists. It has a long and distinguished tradition, and con temporary students of empire need only build on what has already been accom plished. Ferguson and Hardt and Negri thus serve a useful purpose. They illustrate what not to do if one is serious about understanding empire. No less important, they also show just how to proceed if one wants to make a splash in the publishing world. Their books thereby embody the moral dilemmas and ethical choices that all politi cal scientists, at least since Max Weber, have had to face. Readers should, if nothing else, be grateful to them for enhancing awareness of these difficult issues. NOTES 1. See www.amazon.com, March 10, 2005; www.barnesandnoble.com, March 10, 2005. 2.
